1271.quote_or_event: “O my Lord and Master, You alone know the state of my inner being.”
1271.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that the Lord sees what is hidden inside the devotee, whatever is shown outwardly.
1271.tie_back: In the Kural the husband sees through his wife's attempt to hide her feelings, because her eyes speak; Guru Ram Das likewise says the inner state cannot be hidden from the Beloved.
1271.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 735, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1271._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; reasonable but partial: both say the beloved knows the hidden inner state, but the Kural's point that the eyes betray what one tries to conceal is not in the line; the knower here is God.

1272.quote_or_event: “They are also known as 'satee', who abide in modesty and contentment.”
1272.explanation: Guru Amar Das redefines the 'satee' (the virtuous wife): she is honoured for her modesty and contentment, not, as in the custom he rejected, for dying on her husband's pyre.
1272.tie_back: The Kural praises a woman whose modesty is greater even than her beauty; Guru Amar Das likewise says a woman's true honour lies in her modesty.
1272.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 787, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar (salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1272._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; reasonable but partial: both rank a woman's modesty as her highest quality, but the Kural praises beauty and modesty together, while this salok is part of the Sikh rejection of sati (widow-burning), a different context.

1273.quote_or_event: “The universe is strung on His Thread.”
1273.explanation: Guru Arjan says that all creation is held together by the Lord, like beads on a string that is hidden but runs through them all.
1273.tie_back: The Kural sees the thread showing through crystal beads as a picture of the hidden feeling shining through the young woman's beauty; Guru Arjan uses the same thread-and-beads image for the hidden Lord running through all things.
1273.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1150, Raag Bhairao, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1273._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match: the thread image is shared, but Guru Arjan uses it for God's presence in creation, not for a lover's hidden intent showing through beauty.

1274.quote_or_event: “Like the fragrance which remains in the flower, and like the reflection in the mirror,”
1274.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur goes on to say that, like fragrance in a flower, the Lord dwells deep within, so one should search for Him in one's own heart.
1274.tie_back: The Kural says something lies hidden in the young woman's budding smile as fragrance lies hidden in an unopened bud; Guru Tegh Bahadur uses the same image of hidden fragrance for the Lord hidden in the heart.
1274.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1274._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; the image of fragrance hidden in a flower is a close match, but Guru Tegh Bahadur applies it to God hidden within, not to a lover's unspoken intention; the continuation of the line is paraphrased here, not quoted.

1275.quote_or_event: “The Holy Saint has given me the Medicine of the Naam.”
1275.explanation: Guru Arjan says the Saint gave him the Name of the Lord as a medicine that cures the soul's suffering.
1275.tie_back: The Kural says the secret sign the beloved gave as she left holds a medicine for deep sorrow; Guru Arjan likewise speaks of a gift from another that heals sorrow.
1275.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 101, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1275._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match: the shared idea is a gift that heals sorrow, but the Naam is openly given spiritual medicine, not a lover's secret sign.

1276.quote_or_event: “Beholding His wondrous beauty, the milk-maid was entranced, and said, "Please don't leave me; please don't come and go!"”
1276.explanation: Kabir pictures a milk-maid so captivated by the Lord's beauty that, even while with Him, she begs Him not to leave.
1276.tie_back: In the Kural the wife reads her husband's unusually loving embrace as a hint that he means to leave again; Kabir's milk-maid, too, feels the fear of parting in the very moment of closeness.
1276.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 338, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1276._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; reasonable but partial: both join closeness with fear of parting, but the Kural's suspicion that great tenderness signals coming separation is not in Kabir; the love is devotional, not romantic.

1277.quote_or_event: “The soul-bride has grown weak, in the pain of separation from her Husband Lord.”
1277.explanation: Guru Nanak describes the soul-bride's body wasting with the pain of being apart from the Lord.
1277.tie_back: In the Kural the wife's bangles slip from her thinned wrists, showing the parting before she admits it; Guru Nanak likewise shows separation written on the body of the soul-bride.
1277.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 242, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1277._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; reasonable but partial: both show separation weakening the body, but the Kural's point that the bangles knew before she did has no parallel; the love is spiritual.

1278.quote_or_event: “The soul-bride is wasting away, in the pain of separation from her Husband; how can she see Him with her eyes?”
1278.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures the soul-bride worn down by separation and longing to see her Husband Lord.
1278.tie_back: The Kural's wife has grown pale in a single day as if a week had passed since he left; Guru Nanak's soul-bride is likewise visibly wasting from the pain of separation.
1278.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 242, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1278._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; a fair fit on the body visibly wasting from separation, though the Kural's contrast of one day against seven is absent and the love is spiritual, not romantic.

1279.quote_or_event: “I tell them the state of my soul, and pray that I may be united with the Sovereign Lord King, my Friend.”
1279.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the seeker who tells the holy ones the state of her soul and asks them to help her meet the Beloved.
1279.tie_back: In the Kural the confidante explains the heroine's silent gestures to the husband; Guru Arjan likewise has the inner state made known through a go-between so that union may come.
1279.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 958, Raag Raamkalee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1279._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match: both involve a go-between who conveys the lover's inner state, but the Kural's wordless signs (looking at bangles, shoulders, feet) have no parallel, and here the state is told in words.

1280.quote_or_event: “Listen, O my Friend, to my message of love; my eyes are fixed upon You.”
1280.explanation: Guru Ram Das pleads with the Beloved, with his eyes fixed on Him, to hear his message of love.
1280.tie_back: The Kural praises the woman who tells her love-sickness with her eyes and so pleads with her beloved; Guru Ram Das likewise pleads with eyes fixed on the Beloved.
1280.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 302, Raag Gauree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1280._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; a strong fit on pleading for love with the eyes, though the Kural's praise of this as the height of womanliness is absent and Gurbani's love is spiritual, not romantic.
